newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU vows no new taxes on Internet commerce.
newsitem.headline: EU vows no new taxes on Internet commerce.

text.p: A European Union-sponsored conference on Internet commerce agreed in principle Tuesday there would be no new trade barriers or taxes imposed on companies or individuals wishing to do business in cyberspace.

But the conference, attended by 40 government officials from Europe, the United States, Japan and Canada, appeared to make little progress on how to regulate encryption products, which scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key."

The officials agreed Internet regulation should be led by private enterprise rather than governments. They also hailed some of the ideas proposed last week by President Clinton calling for the creation of a global "free-trade zone" on the Internet but stopped short of fully embracing the U.S. plan.
"We have agreed there should be no discriminatory taxes and laws placed on the Internet," said German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, host of the two-day conference.
"The ministers have agreed that there should only be state regulation where absolutely necessary and private initiative and market forces should have as much room as possible."
Rexrodt said he did not think the Internet should become a "global duty-free shop," but he was ready to discuss whether to abolish tariffs for cyberspace products and services.

The officials also agreed that intermediaries like computer network operators and access providers should not in general be responsible for illegal content unless they had "reasonable grounds to know and reasonable possibility to control content."
The document was signed by 29 countries, including all EU members, Eastern European nations and members of the European Free Trade Association.
The United States, Canada, Japan and Russia were observers at the conference and did not sign the final statement.
The main sticking point at the conference was how to regulate encryption technology that lets companies and individuals protect messages and transactions on the Internet by encoding them.

The United States heavily restricts export of encryption technology and requires companies using the most powerful encryption software to provide a so-called key that would allow law enforcement officials to "recover", or decode, encrypted messages.

"We feel very strongly that there must be a balance between encrypting products to protect them and legitimate law enforcement and security concerns," U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley told reporters at the conference.

While some companies say they must be free to develop and use their own encryption technology, some governments, including the United States and France, have said governments must be able to decipher such codes in case they are being used for criminal purposes.
Daley acknowledged that while Washington was generally in favour of less red tape on the Internet, its position on encryption was that some degree of regulation was necessary.

"There are certain legitimate areas where government has to be involved," he said. "There's nothing in your life, except maybe breathing, that government isn't involved in in some way. And even then, it has to be involved to make sure (the air) is clean."
